'''Chuck Missler''' (1934–2018) was an American Bible teacher, author, and former engineer and businessman whose ministry, '''Koinonia House''', built a large following for a dense, cross-referencing style of scripture study. He appears in [[Media and Personalities]] among the thinkers whose frameworks drive a lot of the ancient-mystery and prophecy discourse — notably the angelic side of the [[Alienism vs Angelicalism]] divide.

== Who he was ==

Missler had a background in engineering and the aerospace/defense and intelligence world before turning to full-time Bible teaching. He brought an engineer's temperament to scripture: he treated the text as an "integrated message system" — a single document, authored across millennia, that cross-references itself — and taught it in exhaustively linked studies, the best known being '''"Learn the Bible in 24 Hours."'''

== What he is known for ==

Three strands run through his work: '''cross-referential exposition''' (reading any passage against the whole canon); '''Bible prophecy''', where he was a fixture of the end-times teaching circuit; and the '''Nephilim thesis''' — his reading of Genesis 6 in which the "sons of God" are fallen angels, and his argument, developed in work such as ''Alien Encounters'', that modern UFO and "abduction" phenomena are the same fallen-angel activity in a new guise. That last strand places him squarely on the Angelicalist side of the [[Alienism vs Angelicalism]] line even as he engages the alien material head-on. He also popularized '''Bible-code / equidistant-letter-sequence''' arguments.

== The strong case ==

At his best Missler modeled genuine intellectual seriousness about the text: wide reading, a systems-thinking habit of connecting distant passages, and an engaging, confident teaching voice that made difficult material accessible to lay audiences. His insistence on reading the Bible as one interlinked whole is a real interpretive discipline, whatever one makes of the conclusions.

== The weak case ==

The same confidence ran past its evidence in places. The '''Bible-code / ELS''' numerology is statistically weak and widely rejected, the prophecy claims carried the usual unfalsifiability of the genre, and the alien-abduction-as-demons thesis is speculation presented with more certainty than it can bear. Read him for the method and the breadth, and keep the firmer skeptical questions in hand for the conclusions.
